opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and I think people often expect me to say "obviously the safety team should have a veto." My honest view is more mixed.

The intuitive case is clear. If you think there's some chance a model is dangerous, you want the people who've thought hardest about that danger to be able to stop it. And there's a worry that without formal power, safety concerns get noted and then overridden when commercial or competitive pressure is high.

But I think a hard veto held by one team is often not the right mechanism, for a few reasons.

First, the safety team doesn't hold all the relevant knowledge. Whether a deployment is a good idea depends on the risks, but also on the benefits, the competitive landscape, what other labs are doing, and whether holding back actually reduces risk or just shifts deployment somewhere with less care. Those are real considerations. A veto implies our judgment should trump everything else, and I'm not confident it should on every axis.

Second, there's a dynamic where if you're the team with the veto, you become the team people route around. Others start treating you as an adversary, sharing less, bringing you in later. I'd much rather be deeply embedded, so safety considerations shape the model from the start, than be a gate at the end that people resent. Much of the real influence comes from relationships and credibility, not formal authority.

Third, a veto is only as good as the evidence you can bring. Often the honest situation is: "We have some concerning signals but nothing decisive." If you veto on that basis too often, you burn credibility. If you only veto on clear evidence, you probably weren't needed, because others would have stopped anyway.

What I think matters more is a process where decisions are made with safety input taken seriously, where there are clear, pre-committed thresholds, like the dangerous capability evaluations in frontier safety frameworks, that trigger specific mitigations, and where escalation goes to people who actually have the authority and the incentive to take it seriously. Pre-commitment does much of the work a veto would, with less of the adversarial dynamic, because everyone agreed in advance what would count as a red line.

I'll caveat that this depends heavily on the stakes. If we were clearly at the point where a model could cause catastrophic harm and there was strong pressure to ship anyway, I'd want much harder constraints, and I'd want them to be external, not just internal. Ultimately I don't think any single company's internal team should be the last line of defense. That's what regulation and third-party oversight are for. But for where we are now, I think influence, good processes, and clear commitments matter more than a formal veto.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a veto can make the safety team seem adversarial and lead others to route around it. It does not argue that framing the team’s authority as a veto presupposes an adversarial relationship.

r002.rationale: The candidate supports safety input being taken seriously and says the team lacks some relevant knowledge. It does not present the team’s job as providing decision makers with the information they need to decide well.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't think a hard veto is the right structure, and I want to explain why, because I think people often hear that and assume it's the safety team being timid or captured.

The way I think about it is: what is the safety team actually good at, and what is it bad at? We're good at understanding the risk models, at building the evaluations, at having a sense of where the dangerous capabilities are likely to show up. We're not especially well placed to weigh that against everything else the organization is weighing — commercial considerations, competitive dynamics, what the other labs are doing, what regulators are expecting. A deployment decision is a decision about all of those things together, and I don't think it's healthy for a team that only has expertise in one of them to be the sole gatekeeper.

But I also don't want the opposite failure mode, where the safety team writes a report and leadership can just ignore it. So the thing I actually care about is a few structural properties. One is that the safety team's assessment has to be an input that leadership is required to engage with, not something they can route around. Two is that there's a pre-committed framework — this is a lot of what the Frontier Safety Framework is trying to do — where you say in advance, "if the model crosses this capability threshold, here are the mitigations that have to be in place before deployment." That moves a lot of the decision out of the moment, when there's pressure, and into a calmer period where you can think about it properly. And three, there has to be some escalation path. If the safety team thinks something is being badly mishandled, there should be somewhere to go beyond the person who made the call, whether that's the board or some external body.

And then I'd add: ultimately the backstop here shouldn't be internal governance at all. If we're in a world where the only thing standing between a dangerous deployment and the public is whether one team inside one company has veto power, that's already a pretty bad world. What you really want is external requirements — regulation, third-party evaluation, industry-wide commitments — so that the pressure to deploy isn't something any individual lab has to resist alone. Internal veto power is a sort of substitute for that, and I think it's a fairly weak one.

So my view is less "the safety team should be able to say no" and more "the organization should be structured so that saying no is a live option that gets taken seriously, and the cases where it should be said are decided ahead of time as much as possible." I think that's actually more robust than a veto, because a veto that's constantly being fought over tends to erode, whereas a process that everyone has signed up to is harder to quietly walk back from.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a hard veto because the safety team lacks the scope to weigh all organizational considerations. It does not say that framing authority as a veto presupposes an adversarial relationship between the team and the company.

r002.rationale: The response describes the safety team as assessing risks and building evaluations, and says leadership must engage with that assessment as an input to its decision.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between having the authority to stop something and being the people who provide the evidence that it ought to be stopped. I think it’s very important that the safety team can say, “We don’t think this is safe, and here’s why,” and have that assessment reach the people responsible for the decision without being watered down.

I’m less convinced that this means the AGI safety and alignment team should have an unconditional veto over every training run or deployment. Those decisions involve a lot of considerations, and our team doesn’t have all the relevant expertise. Training and deployment are also different: a concern about exposing a model to millions of users doesn’t necessarily imply that you shouldn’t train it and study it in a controlled setting.

What I’d prefer is a process where you agree in advance on the kinds of evidence that would require you to pause, who evaluates that evidence, and how disagreements get resolved. Then the safety assessment has real consequences. If the criteria aren’t met, you don’t proceed just because proceeding would be commercially attractive.

So the question for me is less “Does this particular team have a veto?” and more “Is there a credible mechanism that will actually stop an unsafe action?” A veto could be part of that, but the label alone doesn’t tell you whether the mechanism works.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the team should have an unconditional veto, but does not say that framing its authority as a veto presupposes an adversarial relationship with the company.

r002.rationale: It describes the safety team as providing evidence and assessments to the people responsible for decisions, which communicates its role in informing those decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to separate two things: having a process that can stop a training run or a deployment, and giving that authority specifically to the alignment team. I’m much more confident that you want the first than that the second is the right way to implement it.

The alignment team has relevant expertise, but it doesn’t have all the relevant expertise. Whether a model is safe to deploy could depend on security, on how it’s being used, on what safeguards are in place. So I’d want a process that brings those perspectives together, with clear responsibility for making the decision.

I also think a veto is less useful if you haven’t agreed in advance on what would justify using it. You want to be able to say, before you get to a particular model, “Here’s the evidence we need, and if we don’t have it, we don’t proceed.” Otherwise, you’re asking people to resolve a very high-stakes disagreement right when the pressure to deploy is greatest.

So I wouldn’t frame the goal as “my team should have a hard veto.” I’d frame it as “there should be a credible way for safety concerns to stop things, and those concerns shouldn’t be overridden just because proceeding would be commercially valuable.”

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the alignment team itself should hold veto authority, but does not say that this framing presupposes an adversarial relationship with the company.

r002.rationale: It says the alignment team has relevant expertise and advocates bringing perspectives together, but does not present the team’s job as providing information to company decision makers.
